The repeater did not answer your transmissions from here, although it answers you elsewhere. Try high power or a better spot.

Find out where your repeaters really work. With logging on, the app remembers how strong each repeater is wherever you hear it, and whether it answers when you transmit. Drive or walk around normally; the map fills in.

Two layers: Heard shows the repeater\'s signal reaching you, in colour from weak blue to strong red. Key-ups shows where your own transmissions opened the repeater (green) or got no reply (red), which is usually the shorter range.
It works on channels that have a location, which channels added from Nearby repeaters already have. Nothing is sent anywhere: it is all kept on the phone and can be exported.
Heard: the repeater\'s signal at each place you heard it. Key-ups: places where your transmission opened the repeater (green) or got no reply (red).

Heard: the repeater\'s signal at each place you heard it. Key-ups: places where your transmission opened the repeater (green) or got no reply (red). This radio gives no signal readings, so it records key-ups only; the Heard layer stays empty.
On an FM repeater channel: sends your callsign in Morse (about 3 seconds, a legal identification) and records whether the repeater answered from this spot. Use it sparingly.
Sends your callsign in Morse on %1$s and listens for the repeater\'s tail. Only test a repeater you are allowed to use.

Auto fits the height to your Heard measurements once they cover a range of distances (it shapes how far the signal carries over the hills); until then it uses 30 m. If you know it (the tower registry lists tower heights), Set it.
Transmitter power (effective radiated). Unknown: 50 W is assumed and your Heard readings correct the level. NOAA Weather Radio stations list theirs (most are 1000 W).

Range: Auto reaches as far as this transmitter\'s power and antenna height can carry over flat ground (hills only shorten it), up to 50 miles; a fixed range is a minimum. It always reaches your position and everything you have measured.
Terrain heights come from the open Terrain Tiles (about 55 m detail) and are kept on the phone. The first prediction for an area downloads them.

Coverage: the violet pill shows where you have heard each repeater (Heard) and where your transmissions opened it (Key-ups). Turn on logging there; Help → Coverage maps explains it all.
Map tiles come from OpenStreetMap and are kept on the phone for 30 days, so places you have looked at still show without a connection.

Finds the packet stations around you: Winlink gateways, BBSs and nodes. SignalDeck only listens (it never transmits), one frequency after another, and lists every station it hears that is not plain APRS. Nodes identify only every 10 to 30 minutes, so let it run for an hour or two (or schedule it for the night). The radio goes back to its channel afterwards.

Records each transmission heard on this channel and sends it back a second after it ends (up to 26 s), so a station can hear how it sounds, or two stations out of each other\'s range can talk through you. On amateur channels your callsign is sent in Morse at most every ten minutes. Needs the squelch closed on silence (squelch above 0 or Soft SQ); stops when you change channel.
Keyboard chat modes used with fldigi: %1$s. FT8 over FM: the WSJT-X mode on this FM channel, with automatic QSOs (it cannot hear SSB FT8).

Internet gateways reached through APRS: a text message to a phone (SMSGTE, US and Canada numbers) or an email (EMAIL-2), useful where there is no phone signal but an APRS iGate hears you.

Sent as an APRS message to SMSGTE, which texts the phone. A reply from the phone comes back to your callsign as an APRS message when the SMSGTE service knows you (see smsgte.org). Standard message rates apply to the recipient.
Sent as an APRS message to EMAIL-2, which emails the text from your callsign. Most email gateways answer with an acknowledgement; replies by email are not relayed back.

From another radio, key the PIN and then one command digit, as one sequence (a * before and # after are fine). The phone answers on the channel 1.5 seconds later:
Three wrong PINs within ten minutes lock the remote for ten minutes. The PIN never appears in the history. Voice replies end with your callsign in Morse on amateur channels.

An object is a marker on everyone\'s APRS map that you own: a net control point, an event, a hazard. Remove sends it again as deleted. The position starts at yours; edit it to place the object elsewhere.
A bulletin goes to everyone in range (BLN0 to BLN9) and is not acknowledged; most APRS apps list them on a bulletin board. Send it again to keep it current.

Used on the frequencies the app tunes itself: APRS monitoring on %1$s (automatic beacons, auto-acks, digipeats), ISS APRS and its beacon, and SSTV on 144.500. Messages and beacons sent from one of your channels use that channel\'s power.

Sent before each packet while the radio\'s transmit audio settles (it reaches the air about 1 s after the carrier). Flags (the default) are the standard AX.25 TXDELAY every TNC sends; tone is a steady 1200 Hz; silence is dead air. Bench test, 252 packets: at 1.6 s all three decode alike, silence is the weakest when short. Shorter lengths are for testing with your digipeaters. SSTV and DTMF keep their own lead.
Auto-ack is off on this radio: it has no 2 m band, so messages are not acknowledged automatically.
Morse ID after I talk (amateur channels, every 10 min)
Callsign: 1 to 6 letters and digits; the SSID goes in its own box
